analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share repair data and tools with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 45 bipartisan cosponsors in February 2025, the bill cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026 but has not reached the full committee or the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: New cars collect detailed data and require special software and tools to repair. This bill would bar carmakers from locking owners and independent repair shops out of that data and those tools, requiring carmakers to provide them on the same terms they give their own dealers. It would also let owners choose any repair shop, void contracts that waive these rights, and let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners, who could shop around for repairs instead of being steered to dealer service departments; independent repair shops, which gain access to the same repair information carmakers give their own networks; and aftermarket parts and diagnostic tool makers, who could sell compatible products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Bars carmakers from using technological or contractual barriers to stop owners, independent shops, and parts makers from accessing vehicle-generated data and critical repair information and tools [S2].

Requires carmakers to provide owners and independent repairers the same data, at the same cost and through the same channels (including the OBD port and wireless telematics), as they provide to their own dealers and authorized service providers [S2].
Lets owners choose any towing or repair provider and diagnose, repair, and maintain their vehicle the same way a dealer could, and voids contract clauses that waive these rights [S2].

Adds privacy safeguards: anyone receiving vehicle data must delete it on the owner's request and cannot use or sell it for purposes unrelated to repair, with a carve-out only for de-identified research and development data [S2].
Gives the Federal Trade Commission enforcement authority, a complaint process for repair shops and owners, and requires an advisory committee and FTC reports to Congress on repair competition [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers and franchised dealers, who would lose some of their hold on repair information, parts sales, and service revenue, and could face FTC enforcement if they restrict access.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws covering the same ground, which would override stronger state right-to-repair rules, such as Massachusetts' voter-approved automotive right-to-repair law, with the federal standard [S2].
Vehicles equipped with automated driving systems are entirely excluded from the bill's data and repair requirements [S2].

The bill does not force carmakers to divulge trade secrets and explicitly lets them keep cryptographic and technological protections for safety-critical systems, reflecting the security concern that wider data access could open attack paths into vehicles [S2].
Carmakers may retain vehicle data in de-identified form for their own research and development, so they keep a durable data advantage even while sharing repair data [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and everyday: cheaper, more convenient repair options for owners of increasingly computerized cars, and a level playing field for the independent shops most people actually use. The main costs fall on automakers and dealers rather than consumers, though the state-law preemption could leave some states with weaker protections than they have now, and the exclusion of self-driving vehicles leaves a growing category out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, cleared its Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026, and is now waiting for the full committee to act before it can get a House vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Dunn (R-FL) introduced the REPAIR Act on February 25, 2025, with 15 original cosponsors from both parties, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
It gathered 45 cosponsors, 23 Democrats and 22 Republicans, showing unusually broad bipartisan support for a right-to-repair bill [S3].
On February 10, 2026, the subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S4].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee has not scheduled a markup or a floor vote, so the bill has not advanced beyond committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, automakers benefit from the status quo: the bill sits in committee, so their control over repair data and dealer service revenue remains unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, for now — the bill is still stuck in committee

for.what_they_did: Introduced the REPAIR Act and led it through introduction

for.what_they_did: Held a markup on February 10, 2026 and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a full-committee markup or advanced the bill to the floor since the subcommittee forwarded it in February 2026

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.role: Auto industry (Alliance for Automotive Innovation and allied dealer groups)
against.what_they_did: Opposed right-to-repair legislation, arguing it threatens vehicle cybersecurity, safety, and intellectual property

sides.party_line_note: The 45 cosponsors split almost evenly, 23 Democrats and 22 Republicans, and the subcommittee advanced the bill on a voice vote, so this is one of the rarer bills with genuine two-party support.

industries.note: Carmakers currently control vehicle-generated data and repair software, which steers owners to dealer service departments and proprietary parts. The bill would force them to share that data and tools on equal terms, cutting into a high-margin revenue stream.
Shops outside the dealer network would get the same repair information and tools as dealers, letting them compete for modern vehicle repairs they are often locked out of.

industries.industry: Aftermarket parts and diagnostic tool makers
industries.note: Parts makers and tool manufacturers could legally produce and sell compatible parts and diagnostic equipment, expanding choices and price competition for owners.
Dealer service centers would face more competition for repair work as owners gain real alternatives, reducing service revenue that is a core dealership profit source.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship and subcommittee approval, but most bills that stop at this stage never get a full committee markup, and without one it cannot reach the House floor. If the full Energy and Commerce Committee takes it up this session it has a real path; otherwise it will likely expire at the end of the 119th Congress and have to be reintroduced.
